findings.description: The security group allows TCP port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administrative access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or exploit attempts against the instance.

The user_data script embeds a static AWS access key ID and secret access key. User data is retrievable from the instance metadata service (and stored in plaintext in state), so any SSRF or local access leaks long-lived AWS credentials.
No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required" is set, so IMDSv1 remains enabled and an SSRF in the web server could read instance metadata and any attached role credentials.
The instance does not define a root_block_device with encrypted = true, leaving the root EBS volume unencrypted at rest.

The instance is launched into a subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch = true behind an internet gateway, giving it a public address directly reachable from the internet together with the wide-open security group.
The EBS data volume is created without encrypted = true and no KMS key, so its contents and any snapshots are stored unencrypted.
The snapshot is taken from an unencrypted EBS volume, so the backup data is stored unencrypted and can be shared or restored without key controls.
The VPC flow log archive bucket has no server-side encryption configuration, so sensitive network telemetry is stored unencrypted.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, ACL, or bucket policy restricts the flow log bucket, leaving it vulnerable to accidental public exposure of network traffic records.
Versioning is not enabled and force_destroy = true allows the bucket and all flow log evidence to be deleted irrecoverably, undermining log integrity for forensic use.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance in this subnet to receive a public IP, expanding the internet-facing attack surface by default.

The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing a compromised host to exfiltrate data or reach command-and-control endpoints without restriction.
